title: Three dead, three missing in motorboat accident in eastern Nepal - The Kathmandu Post
description: Three dead, three missing in motorboat accident in eastern Nepal  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Three people died, and three others went missing after a motorboat crashed at Triveni in Sangurigadhi Rural Municipality-10, Dhankuta district, on Sunday afternoon. One injured passenger is receiving treatment at Chatara Hospital.

According to the Dhankuta District Police Office, the boat, fitted with an outboard motor, was carrying 15 passengers and its operator from Kopche in Hatuwagadhi Rural Municipality-9, Bhojpur district, to Chatara in Barahakshetra, Sunsari district. The accident occurred at around 2 pm.

Preliminary reports suggest the accident was caused by brake failure. Narayan Ranjitkar, superintendent of police in Dhankuta, said police rescued 12 people, including the boat operator, and took them to Chatara Hospital for treatment.

Three people died during treatment, police said. One was identified as 52-year-old Lila Rai of Barahakshetra Municipality-1 in Sunsari. The other two were a girl aged about six and a man aged around 40. Their identities have yet to be established.

Mohan Sunar, 31, of Hatuwagadhi Rural Municipality-4 in Bhojpur, was injured in the accident. His condition is normal, and he is receiving treatment at Chatara Hospital, police said.

Some passengers managed to swim to safety, while other rescued passengers have returned home, according to police. The boat operator, Suman Magar, 24, of Barahakshetra Municipality-1, has been taken into police custody.

The three people still missing are Shivak Magar, seven, the son of Nita Magar of Kankai Municipality-4 in Jhapa; Pramila Magar, 21; and Manu Rai, 22, both from Barahakshetra Municipality-1 in Sunsari.

description: Will Pakistan players feature in Nepal Premier League 2026?  Yahoo Sports

full_article:
Pakistan players' participation in Nepal Premier League is in doubt as the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) has not issued the no-objection certificates (NOCs) yet.

The 2026 edition of the Nepal Premier League begins on Monday, October 26.

Multiple sources reported on Sunday that people involved with the NPL confirmed even players who had already been issued NOCs were told their permission to take part was on hold.

Some of the group had already landed in Kathmandu when the problem emerged. Others who were still travelling have reportedly put their journeys on hold until it is resolved.

Add The Sporting News as a preferred news source

Will Pakistan players miss Nepal Premier League?

The dispute centres on money.

People connected to the NPL have said the Pakistan Cricket Board asked for US$25,000 per player before releasing the certificates, although Cricinfo was unable to confirm in writing that such a demand had been made to the organisers.

Major League Cricket franchises made almost identical complaints in July, alleging that the PCB raised a $25,000 NOC fee at the last minute when squads were already locked, and several owners responded by saying they would stop signing Pakistani players altogether.

PCB chairman Mohsin Naqvi defended the practice at the time as a legitimate revenue stream for the board.

There is no suggestion of a scheduling conflict here. None of the seven are in any Pakistan squad that clashes with the NPL dates, and none are currently part of the board's ODI or Test plans.

Which Pakistan players are affected?

Sahibzada Farhan, Pakistan's T20 captain, is the biggest name caught up in it. He was signed by Karnali Yaks alongside Hussain Talat, while Chitwan Rhinos hold two of the group in Hasan Ali and Usama Mir.

Player NPL team Sahibzada Farhan Karnali Yaks Hussain Talat Karnali Yaks Hasan Ali Chitwan Rhinos Usama Mir Chitwan Rhinos Iftikhar Ahmed Janakpur Bolts Hunain Shah Janakpur Bolts Haider Ali Sudurpaschim Royals

Four of the eight franchises are affected, and with squads capped at six overseas players, losing one or two at this stage leaves very little room to replace them before the opening fixture.

Boards are entitled to take a cut when their contracted players earn money abroad, and the PCB is not unusual in wanting one. Naqvi's argument that this is revenue the board is owed has a reasonable case behind it.

What makes this different is the timing.

A fee raised during recruitment is something a franchise can budget for or decline. A fee raised after the players have landed, a day before the tournament, leaves nobody with a choice, and the NPL is a far smaller operation than MLC with much less room to absorb the cost.

If the talks fail, it is the seven players who lose their fees and their cricket, not the board. The MLC experience suggests the longer-term damage is worse again, because once franchises start treating Pakistani signings as a risk, the players stop getting picked at all.

title: Nepal party to consider audio examination involving lawmaker Sunar — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal party to consider audio examination involving lawmaker Sunar — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, the disciplinary committee of the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party is gathering additional evidence and may order a technical examination of an audio recording attributed to central committee member and lawmaker Khagendra Sunar. In a written response to the party, the politician denied that the voice in the recording was his and said there was a conspiracy against him, Kathmandu Post reports.

Allegations reviewed by party committee

The review began after Jana Aastha published a report on alleged violence and threats against a woman. The outlet released an audio recording which, it said, contains obscene insults directed at the woman, demands for money and death threats from a man whose voice is attributed to Sunar.

Jana Aastha also said that the lawmaker allegedly promised the woman marriage, made explicit videos and photographs of her, and later used them for blackmail. The disciplinary committee has not yet established the credibility of these claims and must verify whether the allegations are substantiated at all.

After the publication appeared, party General Secretary Bipin Acharya referred the case to the disciplinary committee. The party also instructed Sunar not to participate in events as a central committee member and parliamentarian during the investigation.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Investigative team awaits interview

The committee formed a six-member investigative team coordinated by Hari Chandra Bhattarai, deputy chair of the disciplinary committee. The group visited the Jana Aastha newsroom and received evidence, including the audio recording attributed to the lawmaker.

The group also asked News 24 Television for a recording of the woman's interview for the Sidha Kura program. As of the time of Bhattarai's comment, the committee had not yet received this recording.

According to Kathmandu Post, in the television interview the woman said there had been no violence. A member of the investigative team said that this and Sunar's denial had complicated the review and could indicate a contradiction between her previous statements and the interview. After receiving the interview recording, the group must decide whether a technical analysis of the audio is needed and determine the procedure for further questioning of the lawmaker. Bhattarai noted that an examination, if deemed necessary, could prolong the investigation.

title: Nepal Premier League-3 to begin today - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal Premier League-3 to begin today  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
BY BIBEK SHRESTHA, Kathmandu, Oct. 26: The third edition of the Nepal Premier League (NPL) is set to record a new chapter in Nepali cricket at the Tribhuvan University International Cricket Ground in Kirtipur on Monday, with the introduction of the Decision Review System (DRS), official List A status, increased prize money and revised match timings.

The tournament will open with a high-stakes clash between defending champions Lumbini Lions led by Rohit Paudel and two-time runners-up, Sudurpaschim Royals, captained by Dipendra Singh Airee.

Alongside Lumbini Lions and Sudurpaschim Royals, Biratnagar Kings, Kathmandu Gorkhas, Pokhara Avengers, Karnali Yaks, Chitwan Rhinos and Janakpur Bolts are competing to be the champion of Nepal Premier League 3.

This time they will be vying for a title worth Rs. 15 million. The Cricket Association of Nepal (CAN) on Sunday announced the increased prize money for the top four teams.

During a press conference held at the venue on Sunday, a day before the league’s opening match, CAN Treasurer Padam Bahadur Khadka said the champions will receive Rs. 15 million, while the runners-up will be awarded Rs. 8 million. The third- and fourth-placed teams will receive Rs. 4 million and Rs. 3 million, respectively.

The prize pool marks an increase from the second edition, when the champions received Rs. 11 million, the runners-up Rs. 5.1 million, the third-placed team Rs. 2.5 million while the fourth-placed team Rs. 1.5 million.

Khadka informed that the prize money had been increased based on the rise in NPL’s revenue.

According to Khadka, gross tournament revenues are expected to hit Rs. 1.5 billion, driven by Rs. 200 million from sponsorships and an estimated Rs. 700 to 750 million from ticket sales. NPL-3 had already generated Rs. 335 million from the media and ticketing rights.

"Throughout the one-month tournament, we expect that NPL's gross revenue will reach Rs. 1.5 billion."

CAN President Chatur Bahadur Chand highlighted the league’s potential economic contribution, recalling the economic impact of last year’s Gen Z protests.

“Although the protests were politically significant, they resulted in a major economic setback. The second edition of the franchise league helped revive economic activity in Nepal, and I am hopeful that this edition, with projected transactions worth Rs. 1.5 billion, will contribute to economic prosperity, particularly as the country recovers from devastating flash floods,” Chand said.

Ticket prices have been set at Rs. 500 for general seating and Rs. 1,000 for premium seating during the group stage. Prices will increase during the knockout stage, with general tickets costing Rs. 1,000 and premium tickets Rs. 1,500.

Security has been a top priority during the tournament, with more than 1,000 police personnel set to be deployed daily at the TU Cricket Stadium to ensure the safety of players, officials and spectators.

Police will use CCTV cameras, drones, sniffer dogs and plainclothes officers as part of the security arrangements. CCTV cameras have already been installed around the stadium, with personnel monitoring the area. Footage from cameras at other locations will be monitored from the police control room.

Special security arrangements will also be put in place for VIP and VVIP movements during the opening and closing ceremonies. The Armed Police Force will support Nepal Police by providing security outside the stadium.

With international players joining the competition, the introduction of DRS and the tournament’s official List A status, the third edition of the NPL is expected to further raise the profile of Nepali cricket. The league will also be closely watched for its potential to generate economic activity through sponsorships, ticket sales and related business opportunities.

title: Career judges lose ground as lawyers gain sway in Nepal’s judiciary - The Kathmandu Post
description: Career judges lose ground as lawyers gain sway in Nepal’s judiciary  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
On October 6, the Judicial Council recommended four judges from the High Courts for appointment to the Supreme Court, but left one position unfilled despite having the option to recommend five candidates, including for a vacancy expected to arise shortly.

The council, led by Chief Justice Manoj Kumar Sharma, recommended Ratna Bahadur Bagchand, chief judge of the High Court in Pokhara, and High Court judges Chandra Bahadur Saru, Janak Pandey, and Gokarna Dangi.

The recommendations have disappointed judges who began their careers in district courts and advanced through the judicial hierarchy. Before the appointments, Sharma had said he would give priority to career judges, a term used for judges who enter the judicial service at district level and advance through the ranks of the judiciary. Critics say the latest selection instead favoured lawyers and those appointed directly to High Courts from the legal service.

Of the four nominees, only one had risen through the district and High Courts, and this has raised questions about why judicial experience and seniority were not given greater weight.

Had the selections been based on seniority and judicial performance, Tek Narayan Kunwar and Narishwar Bhandari would have been among those recommended, according to the argument made by judges familiar with the process. Although Bhandari ranked lower in seniority, Kunwar was ranked below Bagchand but above Saru.

Eight High Court judges who had previously served as district judges were eligible for promotion to the Supreme Court. They included Kunwar, Saru, Bhandari, Murari Babu Shrestha, Sudarshan Pandey, Kiran Pokharel, and Dipendra Adhikari. The council has said Saru was selected partly to ensure representation of Indigenous nationalities.

The council’s recommendations also drew attention to judicial performance. Kunwar and Bhandari were among the 10 judges recognised for their performance in adjudicating cases this year, ranking first and fifth, respectively. Neither judge had faced any publicly linked to any controversy. Yet judges appointed to the High Courts after 2013 were given priority.

Pandey and Dangi came from legal practice before being appointed High Court judges on January 13, 2017.

A High Court judge hoping to advance to the Supreme Court said the decision had undermined the expectations of judges who had spent years building their careers through the lower courts.

“We have worked for years in district and High Courts, trying to prove our ability through our judgments to reach the Supreme Court. If the leadership does not value experience, that is unfair,” the judge said. “If appointments are based on picking favourites rather than merit, how can the courts and the quality of justice improve?”

Concerns over the declining presence of career judges in the High and Supreme Courts have also been raised by the Former Judges Forum, Nepal, an organisation of retired judges. In a statement issued on July 31, 2025, the forum had urged the Judicial Council to prioritise judges whose work had already been tested in district courts when making appointments to higher courts.

It was the first time the forum had formally approached the council over judicial appointments. It warned that the number of career judges was falling in the High Courts and had reached zero in the Supreme Court, while the quality of judgments was also deteriorating.

The forum called for at least 80 percent of High Court judges to have experience as district judges and for the same proportion to be maintained in appointments to the Supreme Court.

“Only capable, impartial and honest individuals should be selected as judges to strengthen public confidence in the judiciary through fair, independent and effective justice based on the Constitution, the law and established principles of justice,” the forum said. It argued that judges whose performance had already been tested in the district and High Courts should be given priority when appointments are made to the higher judiciary.

The forum’s position is that experience gained by handling cases at district level and progressing through the judicial hierarchy is essential to maintaining the quality of adjudication.

No career judges on the Supreme Court

Article 129 of Nepal’s Constitution sets out the eligibility criteria for Supreme Court judges. Under Clause 5, a Nepali citizen who holds a bachelor’s degree in law may qualify after serving for at least five years as a chief judge or judge of a High Court, practising continuously for at least 15 years as a senior advocate or advocate, working for at least 15 years in the field of justice or law and gaining a reputation as a distinguished jurist, or serving for at least 12 years in a gazetted first-class or higher position in the judicial service.

The Supreme Court currently has 17 justices. Another position will fall vacant when Justice Binod Sharma retires in November.

There are no career justices on the Supreme Court who began as district judges and later rose through the higher courts. Seven justices, or about 42 percent of the bench, were appointed directly from legal practice. Nine, or 52 percent, reached the Supreme Court through the High Courts.

Seven justices, equivalent to 41 percent of the bench, came from backgrounds in the judicial service, government attorney service, or private legal practice. Four justices who had first been appointed to High Courts from private legal practice later advanced to the Supreme Court. Overall, 12 justices, or about 70 percent of the bench, have a background in private practice, according to the figures cited in the analysis.

The last career justice to serve on the Supreme Court was former Chief Justice Bishowambhar Prasad Shrestha, who retired on October 5, 2024. He began his judicial career as a district judge in Darchula on May 16, 1988, and became a permanent Supreme Court justice on August 1, 2016.

Nepal has had 32 chief justices since the establishment of the Pradhan Nyayalaya, the predecessor to the Supreme Court, in 1951. The current chief justice, Manoj Kumar Sharma, is the 32nd. Former Supreme Court justice Krishna Jung Rayamajhi has described the period under the 31st chief justice, Prakash Man Singh Raut, as the beginning of a “new phase” in the judiciary’s 74-year history.

The idea of a career judge in the modern sense took hold only after the restoration of multiparty democracy in 1990; the earlier system did not follow the same career path.

Bishwanath Upadhyaya, who became chief justice in 1991, had moved from the Law Ministry to a regional court before reaching the Supreme Court and eventually leading the judiciary. After Upadhyaya, Anup Raj Sharma was the only chief justice appointed directly to the Supreme Court from legal practice. He joined the court as a lawyer and later became chief justice.

Sushila Karki and Hari Krishna Karki also followed a route from legal practice to the Supreme Court leadership. Cholendra Shumsher Rana and Gopal Prasad Parajuli became chief justices after appointments to High Courts.

According to Rayamajhi, a succession pattern favouring chief justices appointed directly from legal practice or elevated directly to higher courts took hold during Raut’s tenure. Supreme Court justices Sapana Pradhan Malla, Kumar Regmi and Hari Prasad Phuyal, all appointed directly from private legal practice, were in line to lead the judiciary.

They were to be followed by Nahakul Subedi and Nripadhwaj Niraula, with the succession sequence extending to 2035. Subedi and Niraula reached the Supreme Court after serving as chief registrars of the Supreme Court and being appointed directly as chief judges of High Courts.

Rayamajhi said chief justices and justices must be selected on the basis of merit and ability. Although the Constitution establishes eligibility criteria, he alleged that political bargaining had increasingly taken precedence over the selection of the most qualified candidates.

“Political affiliation should be unacceptable for someone aspiring to become a justice. But it is disturbing to hear that the CPN-UML, Nepali Congress, and Maoists have been allocated their respective shares,” he said. “The Supreme Court should bring in highly respected, independent people. Instead, it has been filled through quotas.”

Lawyers outnumber career judges in High Courts

The declining representation of career judges is also evident in the High Courts, according to Judicial Council figures up to mid-August.

Of the 152 judges serving in the High Courts, 70 had been appointed from legal practice, 56 had risen from district courts, and 26 had come from the judicial or legal services. Judges from district courts account for 37 percent of the total, while those with a legal-practice background account for 46 percent. Non-career judges make up about 64 percent of High Court judges.

Former High Court chief judge Keshari Raj Pandit believes the Judicial Council’s leadership bears more responsibility for the trend than the Constitution itself.

Article 140 of the Constitution sets out the eligibility requirements for High Court judges. A Nepali citizen who holds a bachelor’s degree in law may qualify after serving for at least five years as a district judge, practising continuously for at least 10 years as a senior advocate or advocate, working for at least 10 years in legal teaching, research or another area of law or justice, or serving for at least five years in a gazetted first-class position in the judicial service.

The Constitution also specifies how candidates should be assessed. For district judges, the criteria include the proportion of cases decided annually and the extent to which their judgments are upheld, reversed or overturned by higher courts. Candidates from the judicial service are assessed on seniority, qualifications and performance, while others are assessed on seniority, continuity of professional practice, integrity, professional conduct, and contributions to law and justice.

Pandit said that, although the Constitution does not stipulate fixed quotas for different professional backgrounds, the council’s choices have effectively determined how many Supreme Court justices come from the judicial service and how many are appointed directly from the legal profession.

“When the focus shifts away from career judges towards recruiting party workers and relatives, rather than identifying the most capable candidates, this is the result.”

Why career judges matter

Pandit argues that judging requires more than legal knowledge. A judge’s personal experience, understanding of justice and awareness of the impact of decisions on society all shape how cases are decided.

“Justice is about trust. It rests on faith,” he said. “If that faith is maintained, confidence in justice and judges can endure for years. If it is lost, it can collapse very quickly.”

Political involvement in judicial appointments is not unique to Nepal. In the United States, judges are appointed through a politically influenced process. In the United Kingdom, political consultation is built into the selection process for Supreme Court judges, with politicians consulted at two stages when recommendations are made by the Judicial Appointments Commission.

India uses a collegium system, under which senior judges play a central role in appointments. Yet that system has also faced criticism over continuing political influence, the dominance of particular groups and internal politics within the judiciary. There have been calls to seek alternatives to the existing arrangement.

Former Supreme Court justice Pawan Kumar Ojha said appointments from the legal profession had drawn criticism over growing political influence on the Judicial Council and the perceived unfair treatment of serving judges and judicial-service officials. Such concerns, he said, highlighted the need for balance in judicial appointments.

“The Constitution was designed to allow people with different backgrounds and abilities to become judges, so that people could obtain justice from the courts,” Ojha said. “There may be criticism that the current arrangement is not right or that some groups are being left out, but there must be balance.”

Appointing lawyers as judges is a long-standing practice in many countries, including the United States, the United Kingdom, India, Canada and Australia. Ojha said lawyers bring fresh thinking and can help make courts more dynamic by drawing on their experience representing different kinds of litigants.

At the same time, he acknowledged that adjudication is a distinct and multidimensional discipline in which career judges have an important role.

“Judges need judicial discretion, integrity and ethical conduct, as well as theoretical and practical knowledge of how to dispense justice,” he said. “Experience comes only after long practice. Judges who have progressed from district courts through High Courts to the Supreme Court tend to have that maturity.”

Rayamajhi similarly argued that the High and Supreme Courts would be incomplete without career judges, because cases move through the judicial system from district courts to the highest court. Experience at each level, he said, is therefore essential to sound decision-making.

Advocates of career judges also argue that judging requires a combination of integrity, ethical conduct and the ability to assess cases and deliver sound decisions. A person with honesty but inadequate judicial skills may be unable to dispense justice effectively, while a technically capable judge who abuses that ability through corruption or dishonesty is equally unfit for the role. They contend that a career on the bench offers the sustained experience needed to develop these qualities.

Bijaya Kumar Mishra, president of the Nepal Bar Association, disagrees with the view that judges must have risen through the judicial ranks to be effective. He argues that a person’s ability to deliver justice matters more than whether they come from the judiciary, government service, or private legal practice.

In Nepal, the Medical Education Commission increased the number of seats at public medical colleges by 418 for the next academic year. A total of 9,691 seats were allocated for medicine and other health science programmes, while 77,359 applicants registered for the integrated entrance examinations, Kathmandu Post reports.

Education and Sports Minister and commission co-chair Sasmit Pokharel said the number of seats increased only at public institutions, while quotas at private medical colleges remained unchanged. According to him, the decision is intended to give high-achieving students an opportunity to study at public institutions at lower cost. At public medical colleges, 75% of seats are intended for students studying on scholarships, while at private institutions scholarships are usually received by 10–20% of students.

New MBBS seats

For MBBS programmes at public institutions, 110 seats were added. The Shahid Dasharath Chand University of Health Sciences in Geta, Sudurpashchim Province, was authorised for 50 MBBS seats for the first time. Another 30 seats each were added to the BP Koirala Institute of Health Sciences in Dharan and the Nepalese Army Institute of Health Sciences.

The commission also added 120 seats for BSc Nursing programmes and 98 for Bachelor of Medical Science programmes. According to commission Joint Secretary Hari Prasad Niraula, the seats were distributed among 84 of the 90 institutions that submitted self-assessment forms to obtain authorisation for the next academic year.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Criticism over the programme in Geta

Medical education reform activist Professor Dr Govinda KC called for the authorisation for the MBBS programme in Geta to be revoked, stating that the institution allegedly lacks the necessary infrastructure and staff. He also demanded that the decision to increase seats at the Nepalese Army Institute of Health Sciences be cancelled. In KC's view, launching programmes without meeting infrastructure, staffing and legal standards could worsen the quality of medical education.

KC said that a hospital with at least 300 beds must operate for medical education in Geta. He also claims that the authorities are allegedly trying to count beds at neighbouring public hospitals in order to meet this requirement. The commission, for its part, said the seat allocation was based on inspection reports prepared by expert teams.

The entrance examinations are scheduled to begin on Saturday and continue until November 4. The MBBS examination is scheduled for October 31, the BDS examination for November 1, and the BSc Nursing examination for November 2. The tests will be held from 11:00 to 14:00 at designated centres. They are being conducted about a month later than stipulated by the academic calendar.

title: Shrestha: What Iowa’s prairies might teach Nepal about resilience - Iowa State Daily
description: Shrestha: What Iowa’s prairies might teach Nepal about resilience  Iowa State Daily
publisher.title: Iowa State Daily
full_article:
Every day, as I enter Iowa State University’s Bioeconomy Institute, I pass a display of an enormous root system. It is an ordinary part of my daily routine, something I might easily walk past while thinking about experiments, research deadlines or the next task waiting for me in the laboratory. But recently, amid reports of devastating floods and landslides in Nepal, I have begun looking at it differently.

I find myself wondering: What if some of the lessons hidden beneath Iowa’s prairies could help us protect vulnerable landscapes back home?

As a Nepali graduate student studying sustainable agriculture at Iowa State University, I am learning about the relationship between soil, plants, natural resources and the systems we build around them. My work at the Bioeconomy Institute focuses on recovering valuable resources from biomass. Yet that giant root system reminds me that nature has been developing its own ways of holding landscapes together long before humans began searching for technological solutions.

Iowa’s prairies offer one such lesson.

Before much of Iowa’s landscape was transformed by agriculture and development, native prairie ecosystems covered extensive areas of the state. Beneath their grasses and wildflowers existed intricate networks of roots, extending through the soil and supporting the ecosystem above ground. These roots helped stabilize soil, improve its structure, support water infiltration and store carbon.

What we see above the ground is only part of the story. Much of a prairie ecosystem’s resilience exists beneath our feet.

That thought makes me look toward Nepal’s hillsides, riverbanks and landslide-prone communities with a new question: Could nature-based approaches inspired by these deep-rooted plants contribute to protecting vulnerable land?

Learning from what grows beneath the surface

One plant that comes to mind is switchgrass, a perennial grass native to much of North America. It develops an extensive root system and can grow for multiple years without requiring annual replanting. These characteristics make it valuable in research on soil conservation, biomass production, and ecological restoration.

Deep-rooted perennial vegetation can help bind soil particles, reinforce some shallow soil layers, slow surface runoff and reduce erosion. Vegetated strips along waterways can also help trap sediment under suitable conditions and protect parts of a riverbank from erosion.

Imagine applying these principles to carefully selected locations along vulnerable riverbanks or degraded slopes in Nepal. Could locally appropriate perennial grasses, shrubs and trees help stabilize the soil, reduce sediment movement and complement existing disaster-prevention measures?

It is an idea worth investigating.

But the answer cannot simply be to take switchgrass from Iowa and plant it throughout Nepal. Nepal’s landscapes differ enormously in elevation, rainfall, soil conditions, native biodiversity and slope stability. Introducing a non-native species without careful assessment could create ecological problems. A better starting point may be to study the function of prairie root systems and identify native or locally adapted plants that can provide similar benefits.

The goal should not be to recreate an Iowa prairie in the Himalayas. It should be to understand what makes such ecosystems resilient and learn how those principles might be adapted responsibly.

Roots cannot solve everything – but they can be part of the solution

We must also be realistic about what vegetation can achieve.

Floods and landslides are complex processes. Extreme rainfall, steep terrain, saturated soils, river dynamics, road construction, drainage and land-use changes can all influence the likelihood and severity of disasters. During an extreme flood or a major debris flow, even a well-established root system may not be enough to protect a community.

Planting grasses along a river is not a substitute for early-warning systems, safe infrastructure, sound watershed management or responsible land-use planning.

Yet this does not make ecological restoration unimportant. It means we should understand where it works, where it does not and how it can complement other measures.

For example, carefully designed riparian vegetation may reduce bank erosion in suitable locations. Restoring native vegetation on degraded land may improve soil structure and water infiltration. Deep-rooted plants may reinforce some shallow soils, although their effectiveness depends on root depth, soil conditions and the type of slope failure.

These approaches deserve scientific evaluation, particularly in vulnerable communities where environmental protection and agricultural livelihoods are closely connected.

From a root display to a real-world question

Working at the Bioeconomy Institute has taught me to see biomass as more than a material that can be converted into fuel or recovered for its nutrients. Plants are part of larger systems connecting soil, water, carbon, energy and human livelihoods.

The same perspective should guide how we think about environmental resilience.

What if researchers in Iowa and Nepal worked together to compare deep-rooted prairie plants with native Himalayan vegetation? What if field studies examined which plants best stabilize riverbanks, improve soil structure and survive under local conditions? What if agricultural universities, conservation organizations and local communities worked together to test restoration methods before expanding them?

These are not ready-made solutions, but they are practical questions that research can begin to answer.

For me, this is one of the most meaningful possibilities of studying abroad: learning from a landscape thousands of miles from home and asking how that knowledge might be useful elsewhere. The transfer of knowledge should never mean copying one ecosystem into another. It should mean understanding natural processes and adapting the lessons with local expertise.

Perhaps the giant root system I pass every day is a reminder that resilience is often built quietly, over time, through relationships that we cannot immediately see.

As Nepal continues to confront the risks of floods, landslides and environmental change, we need engineering, scientific research, public investment and community preparedness. We also need to pay closer attention to the living systems that already help support our landscapes.

Sometimes, a possible solution begins not with a new machine or a major infrastructure project, but with a question inspired by something growing beneath the ground.

From Iowa’s prairies to Nepal’s hillsides, I keep wondering what those roots might teach us and whether, by learning from nature more carefully, we can help protect the places and people we call home.

Self-written bio:

Asmita Shrestha is a graduate student pursuing a master’s degree in Sustainable Agriculture at Iowa State University. Originally from Nepal, her research focuses on sustainable biomass utilization, nutrient recovery and soil fertility. She is passionate about climate-resilient agriculture, environmental sustainability and promoting sustainable agricultural practices that benefit farming communities.

title: Nepal to expand flood warning systems across six river basins - The Kathmandu Post

full_article:
The Hydrology and Water Resources Research Centre has published its 2026-27 white paper, outlining plans to strengthen flood early-warning systems, improve scientific research, and promote sustainable management of Nepal’s water resources.

The centre, established in July under the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, has outlined priorities for sustainable water use, climate-resilient infrastructure, aviation safety and disaster risk reduction. The white paper emphasises modern technology, open-data systems, and scientific research to protect lives and property.

The centre was formed by bringing together hydrology divisions, sections and functions previously housed within the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology. It operates under the Water and Energy Commission Secretariat and aims to become South Asia’s leading scientific institution by 2031, according to its long-term strategy.

A key priority is the expansion of flood early-warning systems across six major river basins, alongside plans to lower water levels in four high-risk glacial lakes. Rising temperatures in the Himalayas are accelerating glacier melt and increasing the risk of avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs), prompting the government to adopt a technology-driven approach through the centre’s five-year strategic plan and a separate white paper from the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology.

The flood warning systems will be installed in the Mawa-Ratuwa, Bakraha, Lakhandehi, East Rapti, West Rapti and Mohana-Khutiya river basins under the Priority River Basins Flood Risk Management Project. Launched in 2022, the project will run until 2028, with a budget of $7.54 million. The centre’s white paper also notes that the Bagmati Improvement Project is under way.

The government has also prioritised the GLOF Sanjibani Project, which aims to lower water levels in four high-risk glacial lakes: Thulagi in Manang, Lower Barun in Sankhuwasabha, and Lumding Tsho and Hongu-2 in Solukhumbu. The project will run from 2026 to 2033, with a total budget of about $49.9 million, including a $20 million allocation for the centre.

The initiative builds on earlier efforts to reduce the water levels of Tsho Rolpa in the Rolwaling Valley of Dolakha district and Imja Lake in Solukhumbu. The government plans to apply similar risk-reduction measures at the four newly targeted lakes, according to the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation.

To improve technical and administrative services, the centre has opened four regional offices in Dharan, Pokhara, Kohalpur and Attariya. It has also established two field project offices: the Sunkoshi-Bagmati-Kamala Hydrology and Flood Forecasting Project in Sindhuli, and the Upper Karnali Hydrology and Cryosphere Project in Jumla.

The centre has three main technical divisions covering hydrology and cryosphere science, flood forecasting, and water resources research and capacity development. The National Water Resources Laboratory in Godawari is also being upgraded to strengthen its capabilities in hydraulic physical modelling, sediment analysis and testing.
